newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Hint of real-name amendments boosts S.Korea stocks.
newsitem.headline: Hint of real-name amendments boosts S.Korea stocks.

text.p: Trading in South Korea's stocks turned brisk on Thursday after a hint of changes to the real-name system fuelled hopes that blackmarket money would find its way to the sagging stock market, brokers said.
"News the government may review the real-name financial regulations bolstered sentiment," said Choo Hee-yup, a broker of Dongwon Securities.
Late profit-taking sent the composite index to a close of 678.11, up 3.21 points, after touching a high of 685.95. Volume rose to 41.27 million shares from Monday's 26.96 million.
"Despite the small index rise, volume soared, reflecting the revival of market sentiment," said Yoo Jae-kyong, a broker at Daishin Securities.

New Finance Minister Kang Kyong-shik told reporters he would review the real-name system, introduced to end dubious financial deals. The system bans the use of false names in financial deals and is widely thought to have caused bottlenecks in the economy.
"I think it is necessary to fix the tax code on the real-name system," said Kang, an early advocate of the use of real names.
Brokers said the news raised hopes that funds circulating in the underground market, estimated at 17 trillion won, would flow into the stock market if restrictions were eased.
Kang's remarks fanned speculation that the government would allow false-name trading in long-term bonds, which is now prohibited under the financial regulations.
The speculation combined with news that infrastructure contractors would be allowed to issue long-term bonds in the second half of this year to spark buying of construction shares.
The construction sub-index rose 5.86 percent to 302.16.
Brokers said profit-taking emerged in late trading on worries over falling customer deposits with securities houses.
The deposits are now estimated at 2.81 trillion won, down from a year high of 3.05 trillion in mid-February.
President Kim Young-sam appointed Kang finance minister on Wednesday in a sweeping cabinet reshuffle aimed at restoring Kim's reputation, tarnished by a loans scandal.

As finance minister under former president Chun Doo Hwan in the early 1980s, Kang proposed the introduction of the real-name system, but this failed due to strong pressure from groups with vested interests.
Disappointed by the failure, he left the civil service after a stint as Chun's presidential general secretary in 1983.

Kim, who was sworn in on an anti-corruption ticket, finally introduced the real-name system in 1993. Its implementation sent dubious funds underground as holders tried to evade taxation and government audits.
"The system had more negative effects that positive ones," said an economist at the Daewoo Research Institute.
It was thought the real-name system would enable tracing the sources of wealth of corrupt politicians, but this proved not to be the case.

In a 1996 trial following a slush fund scandal involving Chun and his successor Roh Tae-woo, businessmen who had been charged with violating the real-name regulation were given suspended sentences or found innocent.
"The result of the trial showed too many loopholes in the financial system," said the Daewoo economist.
